chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter XV
paragraphs: At eight o'clock, Kutuzov rode toward Pratzen at the head of the fourth column — Miloradovich's — which was supposed to replace the columns of Przhebyshevsky and Langeron, both of which had already descended into the valley. He greeted the soldiers of the lead regiment and gave the order to march, signaling that he intended to lead this column himself. When they reached the village of Pratzen, he halted. Prince Andrei rode behind, lost among the enormous crowd that made up the commander in chief's retinue. He was in a state of suppressed excitement and agitation, though outwardly calm — the way a person gets when a long-anticipated moment is finally at hand. He was firmly convinced that this would be his Toulon, his bridge of Arcole. He didn't know exactly how it would happen, but he was certain it would. He knew the terrain and the positions of the troops as well as anyone in the army could. His own strategic plan, now clearly impossible to carry out, had been set aside. Instead, working within Weyrother's plan, Prince Andrei considered possible developments and formed new projects that might call for his quick thinking and decisive action.

Down to the left, through the mist, the crackle of musket fire from unseen forces could be heard. That was where Prince Andrei expected the fighting to intensify. "That's where the difficulties will come," he thought, "and that's where I'll be sent with a brigade or a division. There, with the standard in my hand, I'll charge forward and break through whatever stands in my way."
He couldn't look calmly at the regimental standards as the battalions passed by. Each time he saw one, he kept thinking: "That might be the very standard I'll carry when I lead the army."

By morning, all that remained of the night's fog on the heights was a thin frost turning to dew, but down in the valleys it still lay like a sea of white milk. Nothing was visible in the valley to the left, where the troops had descended and where the gunfire was coming from. Above the heights stretched a dark, clear sky, and to the right hung the vast disk of the sun. In the distance, on the far shore of that misty sea, some wooded hills were just barely visible — the enemy was probably there, since something could be made out moving. To the right, the Guards were entering the mist with the sound of hooves and wheels, and now and then a glint of bayonets; to the left, beyond the village, similar masses of cavalry appeared and vanished into the white sea. In front and behind, infantry moved forward. The commander in chief stood at the edge of the village, watching the troops pass. That morning, Kutuzov seemed worn out and irritable. The infantry marching past him suddenly came to a halt without any order being given, apparently blocked by something ahead.

"Order them to form battalion columns and go around the village!" he said angrily to a general who had ridden up. "Don't you understand, your excellency, my dear sir, that you can't march through narrow village streets when we're advancing against the enemy?"
"I was planning to re-form them on the other side of the village, your excellency," the general replied.
Kutuzov gave a bitter laugh.
"That'll work out wonderfully — deploying in full view of the enemy! Just wonderful!"
"The enemy is still far away, your excellency. According to the battle plan —"
"The battle plan!" Kutuzov snapped bitterly. "Who told you that? Do as you're ordered."
"Yes, sir."
"My dear fellow," Nesvitsky whispered to Prince Andrei, "the old man is in a foul mood."
An Austrian officer in a white uniform with green plumes on his hat galloped up to Kutuzov and asked, on behalf of the Emperor, whether the fourth column had advanced into action.

Kutuzov turned away without answering, and his gaze happened to fall on Prince Andrei standing beside him. When he saw him, Kutuzov's bitter, caustic expression softened, as if acknowledging that none of this was his adjutant's fault. Still ignoring the Austrian, he addressed Bolkonsky.
"Go, my dear fellow, and see whether the third division has passed the village. Tell them to stop and wait for my orders."
Prince Andrei had barely started when Kutuzov stopped him.
"And find out if they've posted sharpshooters," he added. "What are they doing? What are they doing?" he muttered to himself, still not answering the Austrian.
Prince Andrei galloped off to carry out the order.

Riding past the advancing battalions, he stopped the third division and confirmed that there were indeed no sharpshooters deployed ahead of the columns. The colonel leading the regiment was shocked by the commander in chief's order to send out skirmishers. He had been certain there were other troops in front of him and that the enemy must be at least six miles away. In truth, nothing was visible ahead except a barren slope hidden by thick mist. After issuing orders in the commander in chief's name to correct this oversight, Prince Andrei galloped back. Kutuzov was still in the same place, his heavy body sagging wearily in the saddle, yawning with closed eyes. The troops had stopped and now stood with the butts of their muskets resting on the ground.
"All right, all right!" he said to Prince Andrei, then turned to a general who, watch in hand, was insisting it was time to move since all the left-flank columns had already gone down.
"Plenty of time, your excellency," Kutuzov muttered through a yawn. "Plenty of time," he repeated.

Just then, from somewhere behind Kutuzov, came the sound of regiments cheering, and the wave of salutes rolled rapidly closer along the whole extended line of advancing Russian columns. Clearly, whoever they were greeting was riding quickly. When the soldiers in the regiment nearest Kutuzov began to shout, he moved off to the side a little and looked back with a frown. A squadron-like group of horsemen in various uniforms came galloping along the road from Pratzen. Two of them rode ahead, side by side, at full gallop. One wore a black uniform with white plumes and rode a short-tailed chestnut horse; the other wore white and rode a black horse. These were the two Emperors, followed by their entourages. Kutuzov, putting on the manner of a grizzled old soldier at the front, called out "Attention!" and rode up to the Emperors with a salute. His entire appearance and demeanor were suddenly transformed. He adopted the air of a subordinate who obeys without question. With a show of deference that clearly struck Alexander as excessive, he rode up and saluted.

This unpleasant impression merely passed across the young and joyful face of the Emperor like a wisp of haze drifting over a clear sky, and was gone. After his illness, he looked somewhat thinner than he had on the field of Olmutz, where Bolkonsky had first seen him abroad. But there was still the same captivating blend of majesty and gentleness in his fine gray eyes, and on his delicate lips the same ability to shift expression, with the same prevailing look of warmhearted, innocent youth.

At the Olmutz review, he had seemed more majestic; here he seemed brighter and more full of energy. He was slightly flushed from galloping two miles, and as he reined in his horse, he sighed with relief and looked around at his companions — all of them as young and animated as himself. Czartoryski, Novosiltsev, Prince Volkonsky, Strogonov, and the rest — all richly dressed, cheerful young men on splendid, well-groomed, barely warm horses — had stopped behind the Emperor, exchanging remarks and smiling. Emperor Francis, a rosy, long-faced young man, sat very straight on his handsome black horse, looking about in a leisurely and preoccupied way. He beckoned to one of his white-uniformed adjutants and asked some question. "He's probably asking what time they set out," thought Prince Andrei, watching this old acquaintance with a smile he couldn't suppress as he recalled his reception at Brunn. Among the two Emperors' retinues were the finest young orderly officers from the Guard and line regiments, both Russian and Austrian. Mixed in among them were grooms leading the Tsar's beautiful reserve horses draped in embroidered cloths.

The way a gust of fresh air from the fields sweeps into a stuffy room when a window is opened — that was how a rush of youthfulness, energy, and confidence reached Kutuzov's gloomy staff as all these brilliant young men came galloping up.
"Why haven't you started, Mikhail Ilarionovich?" Emperor Alexander asked Kutuzov quickly, at the same time casting a courteous glance at Emperor Francis.
"I'm waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov answered, bowing forward respectfully.
The Emperor frowned slightly and leaned his ear forward as if he hadn't quite heard.
"Waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov repeated. (Prince Andrei noticed that Kutuzov's upper lip twitched unnaturally as he said the word "waiting.") "Not all the columns have formed up yet, Your Majesty."
The Tsar heard but clearly didn't like the reply. He shrugged his somewhat rounded shoulders and glanced at Novosiltsev, who stood nearby, as if to complain about Kutuzov.

"You know, Mikhail Ilarionovich, we're not on the parade ground, where the review doesn't begin until all the troops are assembled," the Tsar said with another glance at Emperor Francis, as if inviting him — if not to join in — at least to listen. But Emperor Francis continued to look around and didn't seem to be listening.

"That is exactly why I have not begun, sire," Kutuzov said in a loud, clear voice, evidently making sure he would not go unheard, and again something in his face twitched. "That is exactly why I have not begun, sire — because we are not on parade and not on the Empress's Field." He spoke clearly and distinctly.
Everyone in the Emperor's retinue exchanged quick glances of displeasure and reproach. "Old as he may be, he shouldn't — he absolutely shouldn't — speak like that," their looks seemed to say.

The Tsar stared intently at Kutuzov's face, waiting for him to say something more. But Kutuzov, with his head respectfully bowed, appeared to be waiting as well. The silence stretched on for about a minute.
"However, if you command it, Your Majesty," Kutuzov said at last, raising his head and resuming his former tone — that of a dull, unquestioning, obedient general.
He nudged his horse forward and, calling over Miloradovich, the column commander, gave him the order to advance.
The troops began moving again, and two battalions of the Novgorod regiment and one of the Apsheron regiment marched past the Emperor.

As the Apsheron battalion went by, the red-faced Miloradovich — without his greatcoat, medals pinned to his chest, and a huge plume in his cocked hat worn sideways with corners pointing front and back — galloped energetically forward and reined in his horse before the Emperor with a dashing salute.
"God be with you, General!" said the Emperor.
[Speaking in French] "Indeed, sire, we shall do everything in our power, sire," he answered cheerfully, though his poor French drew ironic smiles from the gentlemen in the Tsar's entourage.
Footnote: "Indeed, Sire, we shall do everything it is possible to do, Sire."

Miloradovich wheeled his horse sharply and positioned himself just behind the Emperor. The Apsheron soldiers, energized by the Tsar's presence, marched past the Emperors and their suites at a bold, brisk pace, keeping perfect step.

"Lads!" Miloradovich shouted in a loud, confident, and cheerful voice — so carried away by the sound of gunfire, the prospect of battle, and the sight of the gallant Apsherons (his old comrades from Suvorov's campaigns, now marching so splendidly past the Emperors) that he forgot the sovereigns were right there. "Lads, it's not the first village you've had to take!" he cried.
"Glad to do our best!" the soldiers shouted back.

The Emperor's horse startled at the sudden cry. This was the same horse that had carried the sovereign through reviews in Russia, and it carried him here too on the field of Austerlitz, bearing the absent-minded kicks of his left foot and pricking its ears at the sound of gunfire — just as it had done on the Empress's Field — without understanding the meaning of the shots, or the proximity of Emperor Francis's black horse, or anything that was being said, thought, and felt by its rider that day.
The Emperor turned with a smile to one of his attendants and said something, pointing at the brave Apsherons.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter XVI
paragraphs: Kutuzov, accompanied by his adjutants, rode at a walk behind the carabiniers.

After less than half a mile, he stopped at an isolated, abandoned building that had probably once been a roadside inn, at a fork where two roads diverged. Both roads led downhill, and troops were marching along each of them.

The fog had started to thin, and enemy forces were dimly visible about a mile and a half away on the opposite heights. Down to the left, the firing grew more distinct. Kutuzov had stopped and was speaking with an Austrian general. Prince Andrei, riding a little behind, turned to an adjutant and asked to borrow a field glass.
"Look, look!" the adjutant said, staring not at the distant troops but down the hill in front of them. "It's the French!"

The two generals and the adjutant all grabbed at the field glass, trying to snatch it from one another. The look on every face suddenly turned to horror. The French were supposed to be a mile and a half away, but had appeared just in front of them — suddenly and without warning.
"Is that the enemy? No! Yes, look — it is! For certain. But how can that be?" different voices said.
With his naked eye, Prince Andrei could see below them, to the right, not more than five hundred paces from where Kutuzov stood, a dense French column advancing toward the Apsheron regiment.
"This is it! The decisive moment has come. My turn has arrived," Prince Andrei thought, and spurring his horse, he rode up to Kutuzov.

"The Apsherons must be stopped, your excellency!" he shouted. But at that very instant a cloud of smoke billowed in every direction, gunfire erupted at close range, and a voice of raw, terrified panic — barely two steps from Prince Andrei — screamed: "Brothers! We're done for!" And at that, as if on command, everyone began to run.

Confused and swelling crowds were streaming back toward the place where, just five minutes earlier, the troops had marched past the Emperors. It would have been impossible to stop that tide — you couldn't even avoid being swept along with it. Bolkonsky could only try not to lose touch with the retreating mass as he looked around in bewilderment, unable to grasp what was happening ahead. Nesvitsky, red-faced and angry, looking nothing like himself, was shouting at Kutuzov that he would certainly be taken prisoner if he didn't ride away immediately. Kutuzov stayed where he was. Without answering, he pulled out a handkerchief. Blood was flowing from his cheek. Prince Andrei forced his way to him.
"You're wounded?" he asked, barely managing to control the trembling of his jaw.

"The wound isn't here — it's there!" Kutuzov said, pressing the handkerchief to his wounded cheek and pointing at the fleeing soldiers. "Stop them!" he shouted, and at almost the same moment — probably realizing that stopping them was impossible — he spurred his horse and rode to the right.
A fresh wave of the fleeing mob caught him and carried him along with it.

The troops were running in such a dense mass that once you were caught among them, it was nearly impossible to get free. One man was shouting, "Move! Why are you blocking us?" Another, in the same spot, spun around and fired into the air. A third was hitting the horse Kutuzov himself was riding. With great difficulty, Kutuzov managed to break away to the left of the stampede. His suite was now reduced by more than half. They rode toward the sound of nearby artillery fire. Having also fought his way out of the flood of fugitives, Prince Andrei tried to keep close to Kutuzov. Through the smoke on the hillside, he could see a Russian battery still firing, with French soldiers running toward it. Higher up stood Russian infantry that was neither advancing to protect the battery nor retreating with the fleeing crowd. A mounted general broke away from the infantry and rode up to Kutuzov. Of his original suite, only four men remained. They were all pale, exchanging silent looks.

"Stop those cowards!" Kutuzov gasped to the regimental commander, pointing at the fleeing soldiers. But at that very instant — as if to punish him for those words — bullets came whistling across the regiment and across Kutuzov's group like a flock of small birds.

The French had attacked the battery and, spotting Kutuzov, were now shooting at him. After this volley, the regimental commander grabbed his leg; several soldiers dropped; and a second lieutenant holding the flag let it slip from his hands. It swayed and fell, but caught on the muskets of the nearest soldiers. The men began firing on their own, without orders.

"Oh! Oh! Oh!" Kutuzov groaned in despair, looking around. "Bolkonsky!" he whispered, his voice trembling with the frailty of age. "Bolkonsky!" he whispered again, pointing at the shattered battalion and at the enemy. "What is that?"
But before he had finished speaking, Prince Andrei — tears of shame and fury choking him — had already leapt from his horse and was running toward the standard.
"Forward, lads!" he shouted in a piercing, almost childlike voice.
"This is it!" he thought, grabbing the staff of the standard, and he heard with pleasure the whistle of bullets that were clearly aimed at him. Several soldiers fell around him.
"Hurrah!" Prince Andrei shouted, and barely able to hold up the heavy standard, he ran forward, fully confident that the entire battalion would follow him.

And indeed, he ran only a few steps alone. First one soldier moved, then another, and soon the whole battalion charged forward with a shout of "Hurrah!" and overtook him. A sergeant ran up and grabbed the flag, which was swaying from its weight in Prince Andrei's hands, but he was killed immediately. Prince Andrei seized the standard again and, dragging it by the staff, ran on with the battalion. Ahead he could see Russian artillerymen — some still fighting, others abandoning their guns and running toward him. He could also see French infantry soldiers seizing the artillery horses and turning the cannons around. Prince Andrei and the battalion were now within twenty paces of the guns. He heard the ceaseless whistle of bullets above him, and to his right and left soldiers kept groaning and falling. But he didn't look at them — he looked only at what was happening in front of him, at the battery. He could now clearly see a red-haired gunner with his cap knocked crooked, pulling one end of a ramrod while a French soldier tugged at the other. He could distinctly see the frantic yet angry expressions on both men's faces — they clearly had no idea what they were doing.

"What are they even doing?" Prince Andrei wondered, watching them. "Why doesn't the red-haired gunner run? He's unarmed. Why doesn't the Frenchman stab him? The gunner won't get away before the Frenchman remembers his bayonet and runs him through."

And sure enough, another French soldier came running up with his musket trailing behind him, heading straight for the two struggling men. The fate of the red-haired gunner — who had triumphantly secured the ramrod and still had no idea what was about to happen to him — was about to be decided. But Prince Andrei never saw how it ended. It felt as though one of the soldiers near him struck him on the head with the full swing of a club. It hurt, but what was worse was that the pain broke his concentration and kept him from seeing what he had been watching.

"What's this? Am I falling? My legs are giving way," he thought — and fell onto his back. He opened his eyes, hoping to see how the fight between the Frenchmen and the gunners had ended, whether the red-haired gunner had been killed, whether the cannon had been captured or saved. But he saw nothing. Above him now there was only the sky — the vast sky, not clear, yet immeasurably high, with gray clouds drifting slowly across it. "How quiet, how peaceful, how solemn — nothing like the way I was running," Prince Andrei thought. "Not the way we ran, shouting and fighting — not like the gunner and the Frenchman clawing at the ramrod with their frightened, angry faces. The clouds moving across that endless sky — how completely different they are from all of that. How is it I never noticed this sky before? And how happy I am to have found it at last! Yes! Everything is empty, everything is a lie — except this infinite sky. Nothing exists, nothing at all, except this. But even the sky doesn't really exist — there is nothing but stillness and peace. Thank God!"

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter XVII
paragraphs: On the right flank, commanded by Bagration, the battle had not yet begun at nine o'clock. Not wanting to agree to Dolgorukov's demand that he launch the attack, and hoping to avoid responsibility, Prince Bagration proposed sending a messenger to the commander in chief for instructions. Bagration knew perfectly well that since the distance between the two flanks was over six miles, even if the messenger wasn't killed along the way (which was very likely), and even if he managed to find the commander in chief (which would be extremely difficult), he still wouldn't make it back before evening.

Bagration let his large, expressionless, sleepy eyes wander across his staff, and the first face to catch his attention was the boyish face of Rostov, breathless with excitement and hope. He sent him.
"And if I meet His Majesty before I meet the commander in chief, your excellency?" Rostov asked, raising his hand to his cap.
"You may deliver the message to His Majesty," Dolgorukov cut in quickly, before Bagration could reply.

Having been relieved from picket duty, Rostov had managed to grab a few hours of sleep before dawn. He felt cheerful, bold, and full of purpose — his movements springy, his faith in his luck unshaken, and his overall state of mind one in which everything seems possible, pleasant, and easy.

Every one of his wishes was coming true that morning: a major battle was underway and he was part of it; better still, he was serving as orderly to the bravest general; and on top of that, he was riding off with a message for Kutuzov, and perhaps even for the sovereign himself. It was a bright morning, he had a strong horse under him, and his heart was full of joy and happiness. As soon as he received the order, he gave his horse its head and galloped along the line. At first he rode along Bagration's troops, which hadn't yet joined the fighting and stood motionless. Then he passed through the area held by Uvarov's cavalry, where he noticed preparations and a stir of activity. Beyond Uvarov's cavalry, he could clearly hear the sound of cannon and musket fire ahead of him. The firing grew louder.

In the fresh morning air, what he heard now was no longer the scattered musket shots at irregular intervals from before, followed by an occasional cannon blast. Instead, there was a continuous roll of musketry volleys from the slopes below Pratzen, broken by cannon reports so frequent that sometimes several of them merged together into a single roar.

He could see puffs of musketry smoke chasing each other down the hillsides, and clouds of cannon smoke rolling outward, spreading, and blending together. Through the smoke, he could also make out — by the glint of bayonets — moving masses of infantry and narrow lines of artillery with green ammunition wagons.

Rostov stopped his horse on a small hill to try to understand what was going on, but no matter how hard he strained his attention, he couldn't figure out or make sense of any of it. Down there in the smoke, men of some kind were moving around; lines of troops moved in the front and behind. But why, in which direction, and who they were — it was impossible to tell. Far from depressing or frightening him, the sights and sounds only heightened his energy and determination.
"Go on! Go on! Give it to them!" he cheered mentally at the sounds, and then continued galloping along the line, riding deeper and deeper into the area where the army was already engaged.
"What will happen there, I don't know, but it'll all work out!" Rostov thought.
After passing some Austrian troops, he noticed that the next section of the line — the Guards — was already in action.
"Even better! I'll get to see it up close," he thought.

He was riding almost along the front line. A cluster of men came galloping toward him — Uhlans, returning from an attack with their ranks in disarray. Rostov moved out of their way, involuntarily noticing that one of them was bleeding, and galloped on.

"That's not my concern," he thought. He hadn't gone many hundred yards when, off to his left, spanning the full width of the field, he saw an enormous body of cavalry in brilliant white uniforms mounted on black horses, trotting straight toward him and directly across his path. Rostov pushed his horse to full gallop to get clear of them, and he might have succeeded had they maintained their speed — but they kept going faster, and some of the horses were already at a full gallop. Rostov heard the pounding of hooves and the jingling of weapons, and he could see their horses, their figures, even their faces more and more clearly. These were the Horse Guards, advancing to attack the French cavalry that was riding to meet them.

The Horse Guards were galloping but still holding their horses in check. Rostov could already make out their faces and heard the command: "Charge!" shouted by an officer who was driving his thoroughbred to top speed. Fearing he would be crushed or dragged into the attack against the French, Rostov galloped along the front as fast as his horse could go, but still couldn't avoid them in time.

The last of the Horse Guards — a massive, pockmarked fellow — scowled angrily at seeing Rostov in his path, knowing a collision was inevitable. This Guardsman would certainly have knocked Rostov and his Bedouin horse flat (Rostov felt positively tiny and weak next to these enormous men and their horses), had Rostov not thought to crack his whip in front of the Guardsman's horse. The big black horse, sixteen hands high, shied and pinned back its ears. But the pockmarked Guardsman dug in his huge spurs, and the horse flicked its tail, stretched out its neck, and charged forward even faster. The Horse Guards had barely passed Rostov when he heard them shout "Hurrah!" and, looking back, he saw their front ranks tangled up with foreign cavalry wearing red shoulder pieces — probably French. He could see nothing more after that, because suddenly cannon began firing from somewhere and smoke covered everything.

At that moment, as the Horse Guards disappeared into the smoke beyond him, Rostov hesitated: should he gallop after them, or continue on to where he'd been sent? This was the brilliant charge of the Horse Guards that stunned even the French. Rostov was horrified to learn later that out of that entire mass of huge, handsome men — all those brilliant, wealthy young officers and cadets who had galloped past him on their thousand-ruble horses — only eighteen survived the charge.
"Why should I envy them? My chance hasn't passed, and maybe I'll see the Emperor any minute now!" Rostov thought, and galloped on.

When he came level with the Foot Guards, he became aware that cannonballs were flying nearby — not so much from hearing them as from seeing the anxious looks on the soldiers' faces and the forced, unnatural solemnity of the officers.
As he passed behind one of the Foot Guard regiment's lines, a voice called out his name.
"Rostov!"
"What?" he answered, not recognizing Boris.
"Guess what — we were in the front line! Our regiment attacked!" Boris said with the bright, happy smile of a young man who has been under fire for the first time.
Rostov stopped.
"Really? How did it go?"

"We drove them back!" Boris said excitedly, becoming talkative. "Can you imagine it?" And he launched into a story about how the Guards had taken up their position and spotted troops ahead, assumed they were Austrians, and then suddenly realized from the cannonballs raining down on them that they were actually on the front line and had to go into action unexpectedly. Rostov spurred his horse before Boris had finished.
"Where are you headed?" Boris asked.
"To deliver a message to His Majesty."

"There he is!" Boris said, thinking Rostov had said "His Highness," and pointing to the Grand Duke, who stood a hundred paces away in his helmet and Horse Guards jacket, his high shoulders squared and brows knitted, shouting something at a pale, white-uniformed Austrian officer.
"But that's the Grand Duke — I need the commander in chief, or the Emperor," Rostov said, about to spur his horse forward.

"Count! Count!" Berg shouted, running up from the other side, just as eager as Boris. "Count! I've been wounded in my right hand" — and he showed his bleeding hand wrapped in a handkerchief — "and I stayed at the front! I held my sword in my left hand, Count. Our whole family — the von Bergs — have always been knights!"
He said something more, but Rostov didn't wait to hear it and rode away.

Having passed the Guards and crossed an open stretch, Rostov — wanting to avoid being caught in front of the first line again, as he had been during the Horse Guards' charge — followed the line of reserves, giving a wide berth to the areas with the heaviest musket and cannon fire. Suddenly he heard musket fire very close, directly in front of him and behind the Russian positions — somewhere the enemy should not have been.

"What's going on?" he thought. "The enemy behind our army? That's impossible!" And suddenly he was seized by a wave of fear — fear for himself and for the outcome of the whole battle. "But whatever happens," he told himself, "there's no way around it now. I have to find the commander in chief right here, and if everything is lost, then I'll die with the rest."
The sense of dread that had suddenly gripped Rostov only grew stronger the farther he rode into the area behind the village of Pratzen, which was teeming with troops of every kind.
"What does it mean? What's happening? Who are they firing at? Who's doing the firing?" Rostov kept asking as he encountered Russian and Austrian soldiers running in confused crowds across his path.
"The devil only knows! Everyone's been killed! It's all over!" he was told in Russian, German, and Czech by the fleeing crowds, who understood what was happening no better than he did.
"Kill the Germans!" one man shouted.
"To hell with them — the traitors!"
"Damn these Russians!" a German muttered.
Footnote: "Hang these Russians!"

Several wounded men came along the road, and curses, screams, and groans all merged into a general uproar. Then the firing died away. Rostov later learned that Russian and Austrian soldiers had been shooting at each other.

"My God! What does this all mean?" he thought. "And right here, where the Emperor himself might see it any moment. But no — these must just be a handful of rotten soldiers. It'll be over soon. It can't really be as bad as it looks — it just can't! If I can just get past them — quickly, quickly!"

The very idea of defeat and flight could not enter Rostov's mind. Even though he saw French cannon and French troops on the Pratzen Heights — the very place where he'd been sent to look for the commander in chief — he could not, and would not, believe it.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: Rostov had been sent to find Kutuzov and the Emperor near the village of Pratzen. But neither they nor any commanding officer was there — only disorganized mobs of troops of every kind. He pushed his already exhausted horse forward, trying to get through the crowds as quickly as possible, but the farther he went, the worse the chaos became. The main road was clogged with carriages and vehicles of every description, and with Russian and Austrian soldiers — some wounded, some not. This whole mass surged and jostled in confusion under the grim accompaniment of cannonballs flying from the French batteries on the Pratzen Heights.
"Where is the Emperor? Where is Kutuzov?" Rostov kept asking everyone he could stop, but no one could give him an answer.
Finally, he grabbed a soldier by the collar and forced him to respond.
"Come on, brother! They all cleared out ages ago!" the soldier said with a laugh for some reason, shaking himself free.

Leaving that soldier, who was clearly drunk, Rostov stopped the horse of an orderly or groom belonging to some important personage and began questioning him. The man said the Tsar had been driven past in a carriage at top speed about an hour ago on this very road, and that he was dangerously wounded.
"That can't be true!" Rostov said. "It must have been someone else."

"I saw him with my own eyes," the man replied with the self-assured, slightly mocking smile of someone who knows what he's talking about. "By now I'd think I know what the Emperor looks like, after all the times I've seen him in Petersburg. I saw him just as clearly as I see you. There he sat in the carriage, white as a sheet. The way they drove those four black horses — my God, they flew! I think by now I know the imperial horses, and I know Ilya Ivanich. I don't think Ilya drives anyone but the Tsar!"
Rostov let go of the horse and was about to ride on when a wounded officer passing by spoke to him.
"Who are you looking for?" the officer asked. "The commander in chief? He was killed by a cannonball — hit right in the chest, in front of our regiment."
"Not killed — wounded!" another officer corrected him.
"Who? Kutuzov?" Rostov asked.

"Not Kutuzov, but what's-his-name — well, never mind. There aren't many left alive. Head that way, to the village over there. All the commanders are gathered there," the officer said, pointing toward the village of Hosjeradek, and walked on.

Rostov rode on at a slow pace, no longer knowing why or where he was going. The Emperor was wounded, the battle lost. It was impossible to doubt it now. Rostov rode in the direction he'd been pointed, toward a village where he could see steeples and a church. What was the rush? What was he supposed to say to the Tsar or to Kutuzov now, even if they were alive and unhurt?
"Take that road, your honor — go the other way or you'll be killed on the spot!" a soldier shouted to him. "They'll kill you over there!"
"Oh, what are you talking about?" said another. "Where's he supposed to go? That way's shorter."
Rostov thought it over, then went in the direction where they said he'd be killed.

"What difference does it make now? If the Emperor is wounded, why should I try to save myself?" he thought. He rode into the area where the greatest number of men had died fleeing from Pratzen. The French hadn't yet occupied this ground, and the Russians — those who were uninjured or only slightly wounded — had abandoned it long ago. Scattered across the field, like heaps of manure on well-tended farmland, lay clusters of ten to fifteen dead and wounded for every two acres. The wounded had crawled together in groups of two and three, and their agonized screams and groans could be heard — some of which sounded exaggerated, or so it seemed to Rostov. He urged his horse into a trot to avoid looking at these suffering men. He was afraid — but not for his life. He was afraid that his courage, which he knew he needed, would not survive the sight of these unfortunates.

The French, who had stopped firing at this field strewn with dead and wounded — since there was no one left to shoot at — spotted a lone adjutant riding across it, aimed a cannon at him, and fired several shots. The terrifying whistle of the shells and the sight of the corpses all around merged in Rostov's mind into a single overwhelming feeling of horror and self-pity. He thought of his mother's last letter. "What would she feel," he wondered, "if she could see me right now, on this field, with the cannon aimed at me?"

In the village of Hosjeradek, Russian troops were pulling back from the battlefield. Although still somewhat disorganized, they were in less confusion here. The French cannon couldn't reach this far, and the musket fire sounded distant. Here, everyone could clearly see — and openly said — that the battle was lost. No one Rostov asked could tell him where the Emperor or Kutuzov was. Some confirmed that the Emperor had been wounded; others said he hadn't, and explained the false rumor by the fact that the Emperor's carriage had indeed gone racing off the battlefield carrying the pale, terrified chief court marshal, Count Tolstoy, who had ridden out to the field with others in the Emperor's retinue. One officer told Rostov he'd seen someone from headquarters behind the village, off to the left. Rostov rode that way — not expecting to find anyone, but simply to ease his conscience. After riding about two miles and passing the last of the Russian troops, he spotted two men on horseback near a kitchen garden surrounded by a ditch. One of them, wearing a white plume in his hat, looked familiar. The other, mounted on a beautiful chestnut horse (which Rostov thought he'd seen before), rode up to the ditch, dug in his spurs, and leapt lightly over it. Only a little dirt crumbled from the bank under the horse's hind hooves. He turned the horse sharply, jumped back over the ditch, and respectfully addressed the rider with the white plumes, apparently suggesting he do the same. The rider — whose figure seemed familiar to Rostov and held his gaze — made a gesture of refusal with his head and hand, and by that gesture Rostov instantly recognized his beloved, adored sovereign.

"But it can't be him — alone, in the middle of this empty field!" Rostov thought. Just then, Alexander turned his head, and Rostov saw the beloved features that were etched so deeply into his memory. The Emperor was pale, his cheeks sunken, his eyes hollow — but the charm and gentleness of his face were all the more striking for it. Rostov was overjoyed to confirm that the rumors of the Emperor being wounded were false. He was happy just to be seeing him. He knew that he could — and even should — ride straight up and deliver the message Dolgorukov had ordered him to carry.

But just as a young man in love trembles, loses his nerve, and can't bring himself to say the words he's rehearsed through sleepless nights — looking instead for an excuse to delay or flee when the longed-for moment finally arrives and he finds himself alone with her — so Rostov, now that he had achieved what he wanted more than anything in the world, had no idea how to approach the Emperor. A thousand reasons occurred to him why it would be awkward, inappropriate, and impossible.

"What am I thinking? It's as though I'm glad to find him alone and upset! A stranger's face might be unwelcome, even painful to him in this moment of sorrow. And besides, what could I possibly say to him when my heart is failing me and my mouth goes dry just looking at him?" Not a single one of the countless speeches he'd composed in his imagination — all those speeches addressed to the Emperor — could he recall now. Those speeches had been meant for entirely different circumstances; most of them were to be delivered in moments of victory and glory, usually as he lay dying from his wounds and the sovereign thanked him for his heroic deeds, and with his dying breath he declared the love his actions had proved.

"And how can I ask the Emperor for orders for the right flank when it's nearly four o'clock and the battle is already lost? No — I absolutely must not approach him. I must not intrude on his thoughts. Better to die a thousand deaths than to risk a cold look or a harsh word from him," Rostov decided. Filled with sorrow and a heart full of despair, he rode away, glancing back constantly at the Tsar, who remained standing in the same pose of indecision.

While Rostov was arguing with himself and riding sadly away, Captain von Toll happened to ride to the same spot. Seeing the Emperor, he immediately rode up, offered his assistance, and helped him cross the ditch on foot. The Emperor, wanting to rest and feeling unwell, sat down beneath an apple tree, and von Toll stayed at his side. From a distance, Rostov watched with envy and regret as von Toll spoke at length and with feeling to the Emperor, and the Emperor — clearly weeping — covered his eyes with his hand and pressed von Toll's.
"That could have been me!" Rostov thought, and barely holding back tears of pity for the Emperor, he rode on in complete despair, no longer knowing where he was going or why.
His despair was made all the worse by the knowledge that his own weakness was the cause of his grief.

He could have — not just could have, but should have — gone up to the sovereign. It had been a once-in-a-lifetime chance to prove his devotion to the Emperor, and he had let it slip away. "What have I done?" he thought. He turned his horse around and galloped back to the place where he'd seen the Emperor, but there was no one there now. Only carts and carriages were rolling by. From one of the drivers, he learned that Kutuzov's staff was nearby, in the village the vehicles were headed for. Rostov followed them. Ahead of him walked Kutuzov's groom, leading horses draped in blankets. Then came a cart, and behind it walked an old, bowlegged house servant in a pointed cap and sheepskin coat.
"Tit! Hey, Tit!" said the groom.
"What?" the old man answered absently.
"Go on, Tit! Do some threshing!"
"Oh, you fool!" the old man said, spitting in annoyance. A little time passed in silence, and then the same joke was repeated.
By five in the evening, the battle had been lost on every front. More than a hundred cannons were already in French hands.
Przhebyshevsky and his entire corps had surrendered. Other columns, having lost half their men, were retreating in disorderly, chaotic masses.
The remnants of Langeron's and Dokhturov's combined forces were crowding around the dams and banks of the ponds near the village of Augesd.

After five o'clock, the only fighting still to be heard was a fierce cannonade — from French guns alone — fired from batteries lined up along the slopes of the Pratzen Heights at the retreating Russian forces.

In the rearguard, Dokhturov and others had rallied several battalions and were keeping up a musketry fire against the French cavalry pursuing the Russian troops. Dusk was falling. On the narrow Augesd Dam — where for so many years the old miller had sat in his tasseled cap, peacefully fishing while his grandson, sleeves rolled up, handled the slippery, silvery fish in the watering can; on that same dam where for years Moravians in shaggy caps and blue jackets had peacefully driven their two-horse carts loaded with wheat and returned dusty with flour — on that narrow dam, among the wagons and the cannons, under the horses' hooves and between the wagon wheels, men disfigured by the terror of death now crushed together, trampling one another, dying, stepping over the dying, and killing each other — all just to advance a few steps before being killed in exactly the same way.
Every ten seconds, a cannonball came screaming through the air, or a shell exploded in the middle of the dense crowd, killing some and spattering those nearby with blood.

Dolokhov — now an officer — was wounded in the arm and on foot, along with the regimental commander on horseback and about ten men from his company. They were all that remained of the entire regiment. Swept forward by the crowd, they had gotten jammed at the approach to the dam and stood packed together on all sides because a horse ahead had collapsed under a cannon and the crowd was struggling to drag it free. A cannonball killed someone behind them; another landed in front and splattered Dolokhov with blood. The crowd, pushing forward in desperation, squeezed together, moved a few steps, and stopped again.
"Get a hundred yards farther and we're saved for sure; stay here two more minutes and it's certain death," each man thought.
Dolokhov, caught in the middle of the crowd, shoved his way to the edge of the dam, knocking two soldiers off their feet, and ran out onto the slippery ice covering the millpond.
"This way!" he shouted, jumping on the ice, which cracked beneath him. "This way!" he yelled to the men with the cannon. "It holds!"

The ice held him, but it sagged and groaned, and it was obvious that it would give way — not only under a cannon or a crowd, but very soon even under his weight alone. The men watched him and edged toward the bank, but hesitated to step onto the ice. The general on horseback at the entrance to the dam raised his hand and opened his mouth to say something to Dolokhov. Suddenly a cannonball came shrieking so low over the crowd that everyone ducked. It smacked into something wet, and the general fell from his horse into a pool of blood. No one gave him a second look or thought of picking him up.

"Get on the ice! Over the ice! Move! Turn! Don't you hear? Move!" countless voices began shouting all at once after the cannonball struck the general — the men not even knowing what they were shouting or why.

One of the trailing cannons heading for the dam veered off onto the ice. Crowds of soldiers from the dam began running onto the frozen pond. The ice broke under one of the first soldiers, and his leg plunged into the water. He tried to right himself but fell in up to his waist. The nearest soldiers pulled back; the gun driver stopped his horse. But from behind came more shouts: "Onto the ice! Why are you stopping? Go on! Go on!" And screams of terror rose from the crowd. The soldiers near the cannon waved their arms and beat the horses to get them moving. The horses stepped off the bank. The ice, which had held under the men on foot, collapsed in a great slab, and some forty men who were standing on it plunged in — some lurching forward, some backward — drowning each other.
Still the cannonballs kept whistling and thudding steadily onto the ice and into the water, and most often of all into the mass of humanity covering the dam, the pond, and the bank.
